title: India Takes Shape
subject: Social Science
description: How India's map changed from ancient kingdoms with shifting borders, through British Provinces and Princely States, to language-based states (1953–56), new tribal states (2000), Telangana (2014) and today's 28 States and 8 Union Territories — with heroes Shivaji Maharaj, Savitribai Phule, Sardar Patel and Swami Vivekananda.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: Which ancient empire does the chapter remember for its famous stone pillars?
questions.explanation: The chapter opens with 'the mighty Mauryan Empire with its famous stone pillars'. The Gupta Empire is called the 'golden' empire; Bombay was a British Province and Mysore a Princely State.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: Which empire does the book describe as 'golden'?
questions.explanation: The book says 'the golden Gupta Empire'. The Mauryan Empire is remembered for stone pillars; Madras and Hyderabad belong to the British period.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: According to the chapter, what is an empire?
options: A small village ruled by its own council
A state with an elected government
A large area ruled by one powerful ruler
A region governed by the Centre directly
questions.explanation: The book defines an empire as 'a large area ruled by one powerful person called an Emperor or Empress'. Elected state governments and Central rule belong to modern India, not ancient empires.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: The powerful person who rules an empire is called?
questions.explanation: An empire is ruled by an Emperor or Empress. Governors ran British Provinces, Nawabs ran Princely States, and Chief Ministers lead modern states.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: In the 'India OS' story, how many 'users' does India have?
questions.explanation: The Developer Note says India OS has 'more than 1.4 billion users' — India's population. 565 is the number of Princely States, 28 is the number of states, and 14 billion is far too many.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: In the chapter's 'India OS' comparison, what do the map 'updates' really stand for?
options: New colours printed on school atlases
Real changes to India's borders over history
Software fixes made to Indian phone games
questions.explanation: The book compares India's map changes to app updates: 'India's map has also been updated several times over history'. It is a comparison, not literally about games or colours.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: Before maps had fixed borders, the book compares India to which of these?
questions.explanation: 'India was like a giant game map where kingdoms could change their size and shape over time.' The chessboard idea appears later only as an imaginary 'what if'.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: In India OS v1.0, borders were fixed and never changed.
questions.explanation: v1.0's features say 'Fixed borders not found. Map lines auto-adjust based on battles and alliances.' Borders kept changing.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: Which TWO empires are named at the very start of the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter names the Mauryan Empire (stone pillars) and the Gupta Empire (golden). Bombay Province and Mysore State belong to the British period.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: The chapter scrolls through India's 'Version History' mainly to understand what?
options: Which phone game Indians play the most
How many pillars the Mauryans built
Where the British bought their spices
Why each big map change really happened
questions.explanation: The Developer Note says: 'we will scroll through the Version History to understand every big map update and the real reasons WHY it happened.'

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: Which 'feature' is listed for India OS v1.0?
questions.explanation: v1.0: 'Fixed borders not found. Map lines auto-adjust based on battles and alliances.' 'Clean interface' and 'home screens' belong to v3.0; the dual-layer system is v2.0.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: According to India OS v1.0, map lines 'auto-adjusted' based on what?
questions.explanation: In v1.0 'map lines auto-adjust based on battles and alliances'. Taxes and trade were the British concern (v2.0); languages drove v3.0.

questions.topic: Empires and the India OS Idea
questions.question: When was India OS v1.0 'released', according to the book?
questions.explanation: v1.0's release date is 'Long, long ago before the British arrived'. The other dates belong to v2.0, v3.0 and v4.0.

questions.question: An ancient emperor wins a great victory and makes a friendly alliance with a neighbour. What most likely happens to his kingdom's borders?
questions.explanation: 'If an emperor won a great victory or made a friendly alliance with a neighbour, their territory stretched outward.' Borders shrank after defeats, not victories.

questions.question: What happened to an ancient kingdom's map lines when the ruler faced a defeat?
questions.explanation: 'If they faced a defeat, the lines automatically shrank back.' Stretching happened after victories and alliances.

questions.question: How did people in ancient kingdoms know where one kingdom ended and another began?
options: Straight lines printed on official maps
Nature: rivers, forests and mountain ranges
Lines drawn later by British officers
State boundaries fixed by the government
questions.explanation: 'They looked at nature' — massive rivers like the Ganga or Narmada, deep forests and mountain ranges were the natural boundaries. Printed lines and government boundaries came much later.

questions.question: Which rivers does the book name as natural boundaries between ancient rulers?
questions.explanation: The book names 'massive roaring rivers (like the Ganga or the Narmada)'. The Kaveri and Brahmaputra are real rivers but are not mentioned in this chapter.

questions.question: Ancient Kingdom : Subject :: Modern India : ?
questions.explanation: In ancient kingdoms there was no citizenship — you were a 'subject' of the ruler. In modern India people are citizens. Emperors, governors and Nawabs are rulers, not the ruled.

questions.question: In ancient India there was no Indian citizenship. What was a person instead?
options: A citizen of the whole land
A subject of the local ruler
questions.explanation: 'You were simply a subject of whichever king or emperor ruled your area.' Citizenship, provinces and elections came much later.

questions.question: In ancient India, everyone shared a common Indian citizenship.
questions.explanation: The book is clear: 'There was no Indian citizenship. You were simply a subject of whichever king or emperor ruled your area.'

questions.question: Assertion (A): The borders of ancient Indian kingdoms were always changing. Reason (R): These kingdoms had borders that stretched or shrank based on battles and alliances. Choose the correct option.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R is exactly WHY the borders kept changing — victories and alliances stretched them, defeats shrank them.

questions.question: Which statement about ancient kingdom borders is NOT true?
options: They grew bigger after a great victory
They were fixed by printed map lines
They shrank back after a heavy defeat
They often followed massive roaring rivers
questions.explanation: Ancient borders were NOT fixed printed lines — 'Fixed borders not found'. They grew with victories, shrank with defeats and followed natural features like rivers.

questions.question: Everyday people in an ancient kingdom found out where their kingdom's boundary was by?
options: Looking at the nature around them
questions.explanation: 'How did everyday people know where one kingdom ended and another began? They looked at nature.'

questions.question: The Narmada is one of the rivers the book names as an ancient natural boundary.
questions.explanation: The book names 'the Ganga or the Narmada' as examples of massive rivers that served as boundaries.

questions.question: The book names the Thar Desert as the main natural boundary between ancient rulers.
questions.explanation: The book names rivers, forests and mountain ranges — not deserts — as natural boundaries. The Thar Desert appears only as a wrong option in the worksheet.

questions.question: A friendly alliance with a neighbouring ruler had which effect on an ancient kingdom's map?
questions.explanation: Alliances, like victories, made territory 'stretch outward'. Only defeats shrank the lines; fixed state borders are a modern idea.

questions.question: Select the natural boundaries the book lists for ancient kingdoms.
questions.explanation: Ancient boundaries were rivers, deep forests and mountain ranges. Railways and tax offices belong to the British period.

questions.question: Why does the book say ancient India had 'no fixed borders'?
options: Nobody had invented rivers as borders
The British had erased all the lines
Every kingdom was the same size
questions.explanation: 'Unlike modern states with fixed borders, the borders of these ancient kingdoms were constantly moving' with battles and alliances.

questions.question: Which natural feature helped Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj protect his kingdom?
questions.explanation: Shivaji Maharaj 'used Maharashtra's natural landscape — the rocky Sahyadri mountains and towering hill-forts — to protect his people'.

questions.question: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj ruled which part of India?
questions.explanation: 'A great and just king ruled western India — Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj.' His kingdom was in Maharashtra.

questions.question: Besides the Sahyadri mountains, what did Shivaji Maharaj use to protect his people?
questions.explanation: He used 'the rocky Sahyadri mountains and towering hill-forts'. Elephant parades are mentioned for Princely rulers under the British.

questions.question: Who was attacking India's coasts in Shivaji Maharaj's time?
questions.explanation: 'Foreign traders (like the British and Portuguese) and sea pirates were using ships to attack India's coasts and bully local fishermen.'

questions.question: What did Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj do about the attacks on India's coasts?
options: Signed a trade deal with the Portuguese
Built India's first coastal defence system
Moved all the fishermen to the Sahyadris
Asked the British to guard the coastline
questions.explanation: 'To stop them, Shivaji Maharaj built India's very first coastal defense system from scratch.'

questions.question: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj is known by which title?
questions.explanation: Because he built India's first coastal defence system, 'he is known as the Father of the Indian Navy'.

questions.question: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj ruled long before the Mauryan and Gupta empires.
questions.explanation: The book says he ruled 'long AFTER the Mauryan and Gupta empires', in western India.

questions.question: According to the book, Shivaji Maharaj showed that a ruler's true boundary is where?
options: The biggest rivers meet the sea
The printed map lines are drawn
His people feel safe and get justice
questions.explanation: 'He showed that a ruler's true boundary is where his people feel safe and treated with justice.'

questions.question: Which foreign traders does the book mention bullying local fishermen?
questions.explanation: The book names 'the British and Portuguese' as foreign traders attacking the coasts. Santhals and Gonds are Indian tribal communities, not traders.

questions.question: What makes Sindhudurg Fort special?
options: It is a hill-fort on the Sahyadri peaks
It is a sea-fortress built inside the ocean
It is a palace in the Bombay Province
It is a river-fort on the Narmada banks
questions.explanation: 'This is the magnificent Sindhudurg Fort, a massive sea-fortress built right inside the ocean.'

questions.question: Where is Sindhudurg Fort located?
questions.explanation: The caption reads 'Location: Malvan, Sindhudurg district, Maharashtra'.

questions.question: Sindhudurg Fort's walls have survived crashing salt waves and monsoon storms for hundreds of years.
questions.explanation: 'Its walls are so thick and clever that they have survived crashing salt waves and heavy monsoon storms for hundreds of years.'

questions.question: The book calls Shivaji Maharaj's hill-forts and sea-forts an example of which kind of heritage?
questions.explanation: The box is titled 'Natural & Architectural Heritage – The Living Fort' and calls the forts 'magnificent engineering heritage… our architectural heritage'.

questions.question: According to the chapter's news report, which achievement earned Shivaji Maharaj the title 'Father of the Indian Navy'?
options: Formed India's first navy to guard the coast
Discovered the first sea route to Europe
Used hill-forts to protect his kingdom
Built new ports on the western coast for trade
questions.explanation: The title comes from building India's first coastal defence system — a navy to defend the coast. Hill-forts protected the land, not the sea, and he did not discover sea routes or build trading ports.

questions.question: Which pair is CORRECTLY matched?
options: Savitribai Phule — merged the 565 Princely States together
Shivaji Maharaj — built hill-forts and strengthened coastal defence
Sardar Patel — opened schools for girls with Jyotirao Phule
Swami Vivekananda — created the new state of Telangana
questions.explanation: Shivaji Maharaj used hill-forts and built the coastal defence. Patel merged the Princely States, Savitribai Phule opened schools, and Vivekananda promoted Unity in Diversity — nobody in the chapter 'created' Telangana.

questions.question: What does Sindhudurg Fort show us, according to the book?
options: How the British collected coastal taxes
How ancient builders teamed up with nature
How Telugu speakers won their own state
questions.explanation: 'This is our architectural heritage showing us how ancient builders teamed up with nature to keep people safe.'

questions.question: Sindhudurg Fort stands on a high Sahyadri peak, far from the sea.
questions.explanation: Sindhudurg is a SEA-fortress 'built right inside the ocean' at Malvan. Hill-forts were separate.

questions.question: In which state are Shivaji Maharaj's hill-forts and sea-forts?
questions.explanation: 'The rocky hill-forts and sea-forts built by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj in Maharashtra are magnificent engineering heritage.'

questions.question: Shivaji Maharaj built the coastal defence 'from scratch'. What does this tell us?
options: No such coastal navy existed before
He copied the British navy exactly
He rebuilt an old Mauryan sea fleet
The Portuguese gave him the ships
questions.explanation: 'From scratch' means he started with nothing — it was India's 'very first' coastal defence system, which is why he is called Father of the Indian Navy.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: When did British traders first arrive in India?
questions.explanation: 'In the 1600s, British traders arrived in India to buy spices, cotton and silk.' British rule (v2.0) is dated 1757–1947.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: What did the British traders come to India to buy?
questions.explanation: The book says they came 'to buy spices, cotton and silk'.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Why did the British draw new boundaries in India?
options: To keep each language group together
To give tribal communities their own states
To follow the rivers and mountains closely
To make trade easy and collect taxes
questions.explanation: 'They only cared about two things: making trade easy and collecting taxes. They drew new boundaries to make things convenient for themselves.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: The British came to India first as rulers and later became traders.
questions.explanation: It was the other way round: 'They came as traders but slowly, they turned into rulers.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: What is the 'release date' of India OS v2.0, the British period?
questions.explanation: v2.0: 'Release Date: Under British Rule (1757 – 1947)'.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: What was the 'system style' of India OS v2.0?
questions.explanation: v2.0 was 'Provinces & Princely States — a dual-layer system'. The others are the styles of v1.0, v3.0 and v4.0.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Who ruled the British Provinces and made all the laws there?
questions.explanation: In the Provinces the British 'removed the old rulers and sent in British governors to make all the laws'.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Which of these were examples of British Provinces?
questions.explanation: 'Examples included the giant Bombay Province and Madras Province.' Mysore, Jaipur and Hyderabad were Princely States; Delhi and Ladakh are Union Territories today.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Which of these were Princely States?
questions.explanation: 'These areas were called Princely States, like the kingdoms of Mysore, Jaipur, or Hyderabad.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Find the odd one out.
questions.explanation: Bombay was a British PROVINCE run by a British governor. Mysore, Jaipur and Hyderabad were PRINCELY STATES run by local kings and Nawabs.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: With how many Indian kings, queens and Nawabs did the British make a deal?
questions.explanation: 'They made a deal with 565 separate Indian Kings, Queens, and Nawabs.' Later, Sardar Patel merged these 565 Princely States.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Provinces : British governors :: Princely States : ______
questions.explanation: Provinces were run by British governors; Princely States were run by local kings, queens and Nawabs who obeyed the British.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: What did the British deal require Princely rulers to do?
options: Pay money and accept the British as bosses
Speak English and give up their palaces
Send their armies to fight in Europe
Hand over all forts to British governors
questions.explanation: 'You can rule your local people, but you must pay us money and accept that we are the ultimate bosses.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Under the British deal, what could Princely rulers KEEP? Select all that apply.
options: The right to make all the laws
questions.explanation: 'You can keep your palaces, your golden crowns, and your grand elephant parades.' But they had to obey the British, so they had neither full freedom nor full law-making power.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: In the Provinces, the British removed the old rulers and sent governors to make all the laws.
questions.explanation: This is how the book describes the Provinces — 'huge chunks of land that the British took over completely'.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: The British ruled all 565 Princely States directly through British governors.
questions.explanation: Princely States kept their own kings, queens and Nawabs under a deal; only the Provinces had British governors.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Why did the British make a deal with Indian kings instead of ruling everything themselves?
options: The kings paid them to stay far away
India was too massive to run on their own
They wanted every language to have a state
They were afraid of the Maratha navy
questions.explanation: 'The British realized India was too massive to run on their own. So, they made a deal with 565 separate Indian Kings, Queens, and Nawabs.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: The British let Princely rulers keep their thrones but made them accept British control. What does this tell you about the rulers' freedom?
options: They had complete freedom with no British rules
They had no freedom at all in their palaces
They had limited freedom under British control
They had full freedom to set taxes and laws
questions.explanation: The answer key says the rulers 'had limited freedom. They could manage their own states, but they had to follow British rules and accept British control over important matters.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: The book compares the British 'dual-layer system' to what?
options: Two phones running the same game
Two armies fighting over one battle
Two kings sharing one golden throne
Two types of files with different permissions
questions.explanation: 'Think of it like two different types of files running on the same computer, with different access permissions.'

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Which of these is NOT something the book says the British cared about as rulers?
questions.explanation: The British 'only cared about two things: making trade easy and collecting taxes', drawing boundaries for their own convenience. They IGNORED local languages.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Which statement best describes how the British became rulers of India?
options: Slowly, after first arriving as traders
Only after merging the Princely States
After signing a deal with Shivaji Maharaj
questions.explanation: 'They came as traders but slowly, they turned into rulers.' The Mauryans ruled long before; the merger of Princely States happened after the British left.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: The book calls the British period 'The Colonial Patchwork ______'.
questions.explanation: The section is titled 'The Colonial Patchwork Glitch' because the British map was a 'messy dual-layer system'.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Under the deal, who was the 'ultimate boss' of the Princely States?
questions.explanation: The British told the rulers: 'accept that we are the ultimate bosses'. Nawabs ruled locally but under British control.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Which was the MAIN difference between a Province and a Princely State?
options: Who ruled it: a British governor or a local king
Its size: Provinces were always smaller
Its language: only Provinces spoke English
Its age: Princely States were older
questions.explanation: Provinces were run directly by British governors; Princely States kept local kings, queens and Nawabs who obeyed the British. Size, language and age are not the distinction the book makes.

questions.topic: British Rule: Provinces and Princely States
questions.question: Mysore and Hyderabad were British Provinces ruled directly by British governors.
questions.explanation: Mysore and Hyderabad were Princely States with their own rulers; Bombay and Madras were the Provinces named in the book.

questions.question: In Maharashtra, girls were not allowed to go to school. Whose work helped girls and all children get the right to learn?
questions.explanation: Savitribai Phule became one of India's first female teachers and opened schools with her husband so every child had the right to learn.

questions.question: Inside which British Province did Savitribai Phule work?
questions.explanation: 'Savitribai Phule was working inside the old Bombay Province to change lives.'

questions.question: Who was Savitribai Phule's husband, who opened schools with her?
questions.explanation: 'She and her husband, Jyotirao Phule bravely opened schools.'

questions.question: Savitribai Phule was one of India's very first female teachers.
questions.explanation: 'Savitribai became one of India's very first female teachers.'

questions.question: Savitribai Phule opened schools only for boys from royal families.
questions.explanation: She opened schools so that 'every child, no matter who they were, had the right to learn' — at a time when girls were not allowed to go to school.

questions.question: What important cause did Savitribai Phule work for?
questions.explanation: The answer key: 'Education for girls and children'. Merging states was Patel's work, water sharing relates to Telangana, and Unity in Diversity to Vivekananda.

questions.question: How did Savitribai Phule's work help society?
options: New states were drawn by language
questions.explanation: 'She helped girls gain access to education by teaching and opening schools.'

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about Savitribai Phule?
options: She organised the states by language
She ruled a large empire across India
She was very important for empowering girls
She promoted the concept of Unity in Diversity
questions.explanation: Savitribai Phule empowered girls through education. Language states came in 1953–56, empires were ruled by emperors, and Unity in Diversity was Vivekananda's idea.

questions.question: What rule did girls face at the time Savitribai Phule started teaching?
options: They had to pay a tax to the British
They could not speak their own language
They had to live inside Princely States
They were not allowed to go to school
questions.explanation: 'At a time when girls were not allowed to go to school, Savitribai became one of India's very first female teachers.'

questions.question: Savitribai Phule worked to change lives at the SAME time the British were busy doing what?
options: Dividing the map into Provinces for taxes
Merging Princely States into one nation
Creating new states based on language
questions.explanation: 'While the British were busy dividing the map into Provinces to collect taxes, a remarkable woman named Savitribai Phule was working inside the old Bombay Province.'

questions.question: Savitribai Phule is best described as?
options: A queen of a Princely State
A navy commander on the coast
questions.explanation: She was one of India's first female teachers and opened schools with Jyotirao Phule.

questions.question: Select the TWO people who opened schools together for every child.
questions.explanation: Savitribai Phule and her husband Jyotirao Phule opened the schools. Patel merged the Princely States; Vivekananda promoted Unity in Diversity.

questions.question: Savitribai Phule did her work inside the Madras Province.
questions.explanation: She worked 'inside the old Bombay Province', not Madras.

questions.question: The book calls Savitribai Phule a 'remarkable woman'. Which word best fits her action of opening schools when girls were kept out?
questions.explanation: The book says she and Jyotirao 'bravely opened schools' — she was neither royal nor foreign, and her aim was children's learning, not money.

questions.question: In which year did India become independent?
questions.explanation: 'India had just become independent in 1947.' 1757 begins British rule; 1953 and 1956 are the language-state years.

questions.question: Who helped merge all the Princely States into one united nation?
questions.explanation: 'This was led by a prominent leader, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, who helped merge all 565 Princely States into one united nation.'

questions.question: How many Princely States did Sardar Patel help merge into India?
questions.explanation: He 'helped merge all 565 Princely States into one united nation' — the same 565 rulers the British had made a deal with.

questions.question: After independence, the old British map lines worked perfectly for the new democracy.
questions.explanation: 'One problem kept crashing the system: the old British map lines made no sense for a democracy.'

questions.question: What problem 'kept crashing the system' after independence?
options: Princely rulers refused to give up their golden crowns
Rivers kept shifting the boundaries of the kingdoms
The old British map lines made no sense for a democracy
Too many citizens wanted to become emperors
questions.explanation: The British had drawn lines for tax collection, ignoring languages, so they 'made no sense for a democracy' where people needed governance in their own language.

questions.question: Why did free India need to restructure its states?
options: So the British could collect more taxes
So each king could keep his own palace
So all Indians would speak one language
So governance could happen in native languages
questions.explanation: 'It required restructuring the states to ensure that governance could happen in the native languages of the people.'

questions.question: Which pair is WRONGLY matched?
options: Savitribai Phule — merged the 565 Princely States
Sardar Patel — merged the 565 Princely States
Savitribai Phule — opened schools for girls
Shivaji Maharaj — built India's first coastal defence
questions.explanation: Merging the Princely States was Sardar Patel's work, not Savitribai Phule's. She opened schools; Shivaji Maharaj built the coastal defence.

questions.question: The book describes Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel as?
options: A prominent leader of free India
questions.explanation: 'This was led by a prominent leader, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.'

questions.question: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel opened the first schools for girls in the Bombay Province.
questions.explanation: That was Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule. Patel's work was merging the 565 Princely States after 1947.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the changes described in the chapter in the correct order?
options: Linguistic reorganisation → Ancient kingdoms → British rule → New states in 2000
British rule → Ancient kingdoms → Telangana → Linguistic reorganisation
Ancient kingdoms → British Provinces → Linguistic reorganisation → New states in 2000
New states in 2000 → Ancient kingdoms → British rule → 1956 reorganisation
questions.explanation: v1.0 ancient kingdoms, v2.0 British Provinces (1757–1947), v3.0 linguistic reorganisation (1953–56), v4.0 new states (2000–present).

questions.question: Which of these happened AFTER India's independence in 1947? Select all that apply.
options: British traders arriving to buy spices
questions.explanation: Patel merged the Princely States after 1947 and the States Reorganisation Act came in 1956. British traders arrived in the 1600s and Shivaji Maharaj ruled long before the British.

questions.question: After 1947, what is described as 'the enormous job' that had begun?
questions.explanation: 'India had just become independent in 1947. The enormous job of running a free country had begun.'

questions.question: Which was the very first state created for people who speak one language?
questions.explanation: 'Andhra Pradesh became the very first state created specifically for Telugu-speaking users' in 1953.

questions.question: In which year was Andhra Pradesh, the first language-based state, created?
questions.explanation: 'The First State (1953)… Andhra Pradesh became the very first state created specifically for Telugu-speaking users.'

questions.question: Andhra Pradesh was created for speakers of which language?
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh was 'created specifically for Telugu-speaking users'. Kannada speakers got Karnataka and Marathi speakers got Maharashtra.

questions.question: Why was Andhra Pradesh the very first state created after Independence?
options: It was the largest region in the country
The British left it as a separate area
It had the most wealth and resources
questions.explanation: Citizens 'peacefully demanded a change so they could study and work in their native language' — Telugu.

questions.question: Which Act did the government launch in 1956?
questions.explanation: 'The Full Rollout (1956): The government launched the States Reorganisation Act.'

questions.question: How many States and Union Territories did the 1956 Act create?
questions.explanation: The 1956 Act 'created 14 clean States and 6 Union Territories grouped entirely by language'. 28 and 8 are today's numbers.

questions.question: After the language reorganisation, Marathi speakers had which state?
questions.explanation: 'Now, Marathi speakers had Maharashtra, and Kannada speakers had Karnataka.'

questions.question: Which state was the home of Kannada speakers after the reorganisation?
questions.explanation: 'Kannada speakers had Karnataka.'

questions.question: The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 deleted the old British provinces.
questions.explanation: 'It completely deleted the old British provinces and created 14 clean States and 6 Union Territories.'

questions.question: Andhra Pradesh was created in 1956 as the very first language-based state.
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh was created in 1953; the full States Reorganisation Act came in 1956.

questions.question: How did the government FIRST react to the demand for language-based states?
options: It welcomed it to collect more taxes
It demanded it to please the British
It ignored it to keep princely rulers happy
questions.explanation: 'At first, the government resisted this linguistic change as they were worried it might split the new network into competing systems.'

questions.question: What finally brought the language-based 'update'?
options: An order from the British governors
Popular demand from millions of people
A battle won by the Telugu kingdom
A deal with the 565 princely rulers
questions.explanation: 'Millions of users demanded systems in their own language, and the popular demand eventually brought the update.'

questions.question: Why did people demand states based on language?
options: To get back their ancient kingdom borders
To pay lower taxes to the Central Government
To use their own language in administration
To be ruled directly by the Central Government
questions.explanation: The answer key: people 'wanted to use their own languages in administration and public life and have governance that better understood their regional needs'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 created new states based on religion. Reason (R): Millions of Indians could not access government in their own language under the old British map.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The 1956 Act grouped states by LANGUAGE, not religion — so A is false. R is true: the British map ignored languages, so people demanded change.

questions.question: Why did the 'developers of India OS' launch the v3.0 Linguistic Reboot in 1956?
options: To redraw state borders by native languages
To help the East India Company collect taxes
To force everyone to speak the same language
To build stone fortresses in the ocean
questions.explanation: v3.0 gave 'local languages their own home screens (States)'. It did not force one language — it protected many.

questions.question: What was the 'system style' of India OS v3.0?
questions.explanation: v3.0: 'System Style: The 14-State Linguistic Reset'. The others belong to v2.0, v1.0 and v4.0.

questions.question: Telugu-speaking citizens demanded their own state peacefully.
questions.explanation: 'Citizens peacefully demanded a change so they could study and work in their native language.'

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons the answer key gives for reorganising India's states after independence?
options: Regions had their own cultural needs
To return land to the 565 princely rulers
Governance could become easier and effective
questions.explanation: The three reasons were: administration in native languages, different cultural/regional needs, and easier, more effective governance. Nobody wanted to return land to princely rulers.

questions.question: Select the TWO facts about the 1956 reorganisation.
questions.explanation: 1956 created 14 States and 6 Union Territories and 'completely deleted the old British provinces'. 28 States is today's number.

questions.question: The 1956 States were grouped entirely by what?
questions.explanation: '…created 14 clean States and 6 Union Territories grouped entirely by language.'

questions.question: What is the 'release date' of India OS v3.0?
questions.explanation: v3.0 'Release Date: 1953 – 1956' — from Andhra Pradesh to the States Reorganisation Act.

questions.question: The government happily accepted language-based states from the very start.
questions.explanation: The government 'at first… resisted this linguistic change'; popular demand changed its mind.

questions.question: What did the government fear a language-based change might do?
options: Split the nation into competing systems
Shrink the borders like old kingdoms
questions.explanation: 'They were worried it might split the new network into competing systems.'

questions.question: What happened in 1956 with the States Reorganisation Act?
options: Princely States were merged into India
Three new tribal states were carved out
Old provinces went; 14 language states came
Telangana was separated from Andhra Pradesh
questions.explanation: The Act deleted the old British provinces and created 14 States and 6 UTs by language. Merging Princely States happened after 1947, tribal states in 2000, Telangana in 2014.

questions.question: Which concept did Swami Vivekananda promote across India?
questions.explanation: 'Swami Vivekananda travelled across the length and breadth of the country and promoted the concept of Unity in Diversity.'

questions.question: Swami Vivekananda compared India to what?
questions.explanation: 'He told the world that India is like a grand orchestra made of many different instruments.' The 'giant game map' is the book's own comparison for ancient India.

questions.question: In Vivekananda's orchestra comparison, what do the different instruments stand for?
questions.explanation: '…many different instruments (different languages, cultures, and regions), but when they play together, they create one single, beautiful song called India.'

questions.question: In the orchestra comparison, what is the 'one single, beautiful song'?
questions.explanation: The many instruments (languages, cultures, regions) 'create one single, beautiful song called India'.

questions.question: National Youth Day is celebrated every year on whose birthday?
questions.explanation: 'He believed so much in young people, India celebrates National Youth Day every year on his birthday.'

questions.question: Which state named its main airport the Swami Vivekananda Airport?
questions.explanation: 'When the state of Chhattisgarh was optimized in the year 2000, they named their main airport the Swami Vivekananda Airport.'

questions.question: Why was Chhattisgarh's airport named after Swami Vivekananda?
options: He built the airport with his own money
He spent happy childhood years in that region
He created the state of Chhattisgarh in 2000
He was the state's first Chief Minister
questions.explanation: '…because he spent some of his happiest childhood years growing up right there in that region.'

questions.question: Swami Vivekananda promoted Unity in Diversity decades before India became a democracy.
questions.explanation: 'Decades before India officially became a democratic country, a brilliant young philosopher named Swami Vivekananda…'

questions.question: Swami Vivekananda travelled only within the Bombay Province to spread his ideas.
questions.explanation: He 'travelled across the length and breadth of the country', not just one province.

questions.question: Which statement about Swami Vivekananda is NOT true?
options: He travelled all across the country
He believed strongly in young people
questions.explanation: Merging the Princely States was Sardar Patel's work. Vivekananda travelled the country, believed in youth and promoted Unity in Diversity.

questions.question: The book describes Swami Vivekananda as a?
questions.explanation: '…a brilliant young philosopher named Swami Vivekananda travelled across the length and breadth of the country.'

questions.question: Select the TWO facts about Swami Vivekananda given in the book.
options: He compared India to a grand orchestra
National Youth Day is on his birthday
He built India's first coastal defence
questions.explanation: The orchestra comparison and National Youth Day are Vivekananda facts. The coastal defence was Shivaji Maharaj's; the merger was Patel's.

questions.question: The Swami Vivekananda Airport is located in Jharkhand.
questions.explanation: It is Chhattisgarh's main airport, named in 2000 because he spent childhood years there.

questions.question: Swami Vivekananda said India is like an orchestra. Which idea does this comparison SUPPORT?
options: Many different regions can still be one nation
Every state should speak only one language
Borders should shrink after every defeat
The British should rule the whole country
questions.explanation: The orchestra shows Unity in Diversity: different instruments (languages, cultures, regions) play together as 'one single, beautiful song called India'.

questions.question: Jharkhand was created in 2000 from which state?
questions.explanation: 'Jharkhand was created from Bihar, Chhattisgarh from Madhya Pradesh, and Uttarakhand from Uttar Pradesh.'

questions.question: Chhattisgarh was carved out of which state in 2000?
questions.explanation: 'Chhattisgarh from Madhya Pradesh' — Jharkhand came from Bihar and Uttarakhand from Uttar Pradesh.

questions.question: Uttarakhand was created from which state?
questions.explanation: 'Uttarakhand from Uttar Pradesh.' The other two new states of 2000 came from Bihar and Madhya Pradesh.

questions.question: On which date were Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand created?
questions.explanation: The book's exercise asks you to 'Name the three states created on 1 November 2000'.

questions.question: Which is the best reason why Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh were created in 2000?
options: Their forests had become too small for one state
Tribal needs were not heard from a faraway capital
The British wanted to collect more tax there
All the people there wanted to speak one language
questions.explanation: 'A Chief Minister sitting in a faraway capital city simply could not hear the needs of a tribal farmer in a distant forest village.' The new states gave Adivasi communities local control.

questions.question: The year-2000 'Mega-Update' was designed specifically to give local control to whom?
questions.explanation: 'It was designed specifically to give Adivasi (tribal) communities their own local control center.'

questions.question: With their own states, what could tribal communities protect? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The new states allowed them 'to protect their deep forests, mineral wealth, and unique cultural traditions without being ignored by big cities'.

questions.question: Three new states were created at once in the year 2000.
questions.explanation: 'The Year 2000 Mega-Update — Three States at Once: Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand.'

questions.question: Uttarakhand was carved out of Bihar in the year 2000.
questions.explanation: Uttarakhand came from Uttar Pradesh; Jharkhand was the state carved out of Bihar.

questions.question: Why could a Chief Minister not help a tribal farmer in a distant forest village?
options: The farmer spoke a foreign language
The British still controlled the forest
The river borders kept on shifting
The capital was too far away to hear them
questions.explanation: 'A Chief Minister sitting in a faraway capital city simply could not hear the needs of a tribal farmer in a distant forest village, or a mountain shepherd in a high-altitude valley.'

questions.question: Which state was NOT created in the year 2000?
questions.explanation: Telangana was created later, in 2014. The three states of 2000 were Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand.

questions.question: Which newly formed state lies between Madhya Pradesh and Odisha?
questions.explanation: The worksheet map answer: Chhattisgarh is the highlighted state between Madhya Pradesh and Odisha — it was carved out of Madhya Pradesh.

questions.question: Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Telangana are highlighted on a map. What do they have in common?
options: All of them speak the Telugu language
All were formed by reorganising existing states
All are Union Territories of India today
questions.explanation: 'They are states that were formed by reorganising existing states to create new states' — three in 2000 and Telangana in 2014.

questions.question: What is the 'release date' of India OS v4.0?
questions.explanation: v4.0 'Release Date: 2000 – Present', starting with the three new states of 2000.

questions.question: What is the 'system style' of India OS v4.0?
questions.explanation: v4.0: '28 States & 8 Union Territories — Localised Community Network'. 14 and 6 were the 1956 numbers.

questions.question: Jharkhand : Adivasi communities :: Maharashtra : ______
questions.explanation: Jharkhand was created for Adivasi communities; Maharashtra was created for Marathi speakers. Water distribution was Telangana's reason.

questions.question: Which person does the book give as an example of someone a faraway Chief Minister could not hear?
options: A Nawab in his golden palace
A mountain shepherd in a high valley
A trader buying spices in Madras
questions.explanation: The book names 'a tribal farmer in a distant forest village, or a mountain shepherd in a high-altitude valley'.

questions.question: The 2000 update was made because some big language states had become too massive to govern well.
questions.explanation: 'Some of the large language states became too massive to load efficiently for everyone.'

questions.question: The chapter calls India OS v4.0 'Regional & Cultural ______'.
questions.explanation: The section is 'Regional & Cultural Optimisation'. 'Glitch' is v2.0 and 'Update' is v3.0's 'Great Language Update'.

questions.question: The year-2000 states were created to protect culture and identity. Which is NOT listed as something they protect?
questions.explanation: The book lists 'deep forests, mineral wealth, and unique cultural traditions'. Coastal trade belongs to Shivaji Maharaj's story.

questions.question: Select the TWO states that were 'parent' states in the 2000 reorganisation.
questions.explanation: Bihar gave Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh gave Chhattisgarh (Uttar Pradesh gave Uttarakhand). Odisha and West Bengal did not lose territory in 2000.

questions.question: In which year was Telangana separated from Andhra Pradesh?
questions.explanation: 'The Regional Update, 2014: Telangana was separated from Andhra Pradesh.'

questions.question: Telangana was separated from which state?
questions.explanation: 'Telangana was separated from Andhra Pradesh. Even though they shared a language…'

questions.question: Why was Telangana separated from Andhra Pradesh, even though people shared a language?
options: The people of Telangana spoke a different language
The British wanted separate provinces for more tax
The old kingdoms wanted their ancient borders back
It needed its own government to share water and create jobs
questions.explanation: 'The region needed its own local government to distribute water fairly for farming and create local jobs.'

questions.question: Telangana and Andhra Pradesh share the same language.
questions.explanation: 'Even though they shared a language, the region needed its own local government.'

questions.question: Telangana was created because its people spoke a different language from Andhra Pradesh.
questions.explanation: Both share Telugu. Telangana was created for fair water distribution and local jobs, not language.

questions.question: Telangana needed its own government to distribute water fairly for what?
questions.explanation: '…to distribute water fairly for farming and create local jobs.'

questions.question: Telangana shows that language is not the only reason for a new state. Which TWO reasons does the book give for Telangana?
questions.explanation: Telangana needed 'its own local government to distribute water fairly for farming and create local jobs'.

questions.question: 'The Regional Update' in the book refers to which event?
questions.explanation: The book's bullet 'The Regional Update, 2014' is about Telangana. The 2000 event is called 'The Year 2000 Mega-Update'.

questions.question: Which language do Telangana and Andhra Pradesh share?
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh was created for Telugu speakers, and Telangana 'shared a language' with it. Gondi is spoken by Gond communities who also live in both states.

questions.question: Which is the most recent change to India's map described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The map changed in 1953, 1956, 2000 and 2014 — Telangana (2014) is the latest.

questions.question: Which new state is highlighted on the book's map in the south, next to Andhra Pradesh?
questions.explanation: Telangana was carved out of Andhra Pradesh in the south; Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand lie further north.

questions.question: Which is the largest tribal community in India, according to the book?
questions.explanation: 'The Gonds are the largest tribal community in India.' The Santhals are 'one of the largest'.

questions.question: Which language do the Santhals speak?
questions.explanation: 'They speak the Santali language.' Gondi is spoken by the Gonds.

questions.question: Which language do the Gonds speak?
questions.explanation: 'They speak Gondi and other regional languages.'

questions.question: In which TWO of these states do the Santhals primarily live?
questions.explanation: Santhals live 'primarily in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and Bihar'.

questions.question: In which TWO of these states do the Gonds primarily live?
questions.explanation: Gonds live 'primarily in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh'.

questions.question: The Santhals are one of the largest tribal communities of India.
questions.explanation: 'The Santhals are one of the largest tribal communities of India primarily residing in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and Bihar.'

questions.question: The Gonds primarily live in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and Bihar.
questions.explanation: Those are the Santhal states. Gonds live mainly in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.

questions.question: Why does the book say the Santhal and Gond communities are 'exactly why these updates happened'?
options: Their voices were lost as capitals were far away
They demanded to speak Telugu in offices
They wanted to join the British provinces
They asked for a sea-fort on the coast
questions.explanation: 'Before the year 2000, their voices were getting lost because the state capitals were too far away.'

questions.question: By carving out Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, what did India create?
questions.explanation: 'India created localized administrative systems that brought governance directly to the people.'

questions.question: Which state is NOT listed in the book as a home of the Gond community?
questions.explanation: Gonds: Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh. Odisha is listed for the Santhals.

questions.question: Which state is NOT listed in the book as a home of the Santhal community?
questions.explanation: Santhals: Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar. Chhattisgarh is a Gond state.

questions.question: The new states empowered tribal communities to manage their own what?
questions.explanation: '…empowered these vibrant tribal communities to… managing their own regional growth, resources, and welfare.'

questions.question: Which tribal community's home states include BOTH Telangana and Andhra Pradesh?
questions.explanation: The Gonds live in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Santhal states are Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and Bihar.

questions.question: What did the new tribal states let these communities channel into managing their growth?
questions.explanation: '…to effectively channel their deep-rooted cultural heritage and traditional local wisdom into managing their own regional growth.'

questions.question: Bihar is one of the states where the Santhals primarily live.
questions.explanation: Santhals reside primarily in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha AND Bihar.

questions.question: Which of these is a Union Territory?
questions.explanation: Ladakh is one of India's 8 Union Territories. Goa, Punjab and Kerala are states with their own elected governments.

questions.question: Who governs a Union Territory?
questions.explanation: 'A Union Territory (UT)… is governed directly by the Central Government not by an elected state government.'

questions.question: How many Union Territories does India currently have?
questions.explanation: 'India currently has 8 Union Territories.' 6 was the 1956 number, 14 the 1956 states, 28 today's states.

questions.question: Find the odd one out.
questions.explanation: Punjab is a STATE; Delhi, Ladakh and Puducherry are Union Territories governed directly by the Centre.

questions.question: A Union Territory has its own elected state government, just like a state.
questions.explanation: A UT is governed directly by the Central Government, 'not by an elected state government'.

questions.question: Delhi and Chandigarh are both Union Territories.
questions.explanation: Both appear in the book's list of 8 Union Territories.

questions.question: Which statement about Union Territories (UTs) is correct?
options: An elected state government rules them
They are exactly the same as states
They were created only by the British
The Central Government governs them directly
questions.explanation: UTs are governed directly by the Central Government — that is the key difference from states.

questions.question: Select the TWO Union Territories.
questions.explanation: Puducherry and Lakshadweep are UTs. Kerala and Goa are states.

questions.question: Select the TWO Union Territories from this list.
questions.explanation: Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Jammu & Kashmir are in the book's list of 8 UTs. Himachal Pradesh and Odisha are states.

questions.question: Which 'myth' does the book bust?
options: UTs and states have no real differences
Maps can never change over time
questions.explanation: 'Myth: Union territories and states have no real differences.' The book explains a UT is governed directly by the Central Government.

questions.question: Kyansh says, 'Union Territories and states are the same.' Which TWO points correct him?
options: A UT is governed directly by the Central Government
A state has its own elected government
A UT is always larger than a state
A state is ruled by a British governor
questions.explanation: The answer key: 'A Union Territory is governed directly by the Central Government. A state has its own elected government.'

questions.question: Which of these is the full name of ONE single Union Territory?
options: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
questions.explanation: 'Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu' is listed as one UT. The others mix up separate UTs.

questions.question: Lakshadweep is a Union Territory of India.
questions.explanation: Lakshadweep is number 6 in the book's list of 8 UTs.

questions.question: India currently has 6 Union Territories.
questions.explanation: India had 6 UTs after the 1956 Act; today it has 8.

questions.question: How did the number of Union Territories change from 1956 to today?
questions.explanation: 1956 created 6 UTs; India 'currently has 8 Union Territories'. 14 to 28 is the change in the number of STATES.

questions.question: Which of these is a STATE, not a Union Territory?
questions.explanation: Goa is a state. Ladakh, Delhi and Puducherry are all on the book's list of UTs.

questions.question: Which Union Territory is a group of islands in the Bay of Bengal side, listed as number 7 in the book?
questions.explanation: The book lists 'Andaman and Nicobar Islands' as UT number 7. Lakshadweep is also islands but is number 6.

questions.question: Jammu & Kashmir appears in the book's list of Union Territories.
questions.explanation: Jammu & Kashmir is number 8 in the book's list of 8 UTs.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which statement BEST explains why India's map has changed over time?
options: Maps are redrawn when people want different colours
Changes in kingdoms, languages, politics and local needs
Mountains and rivers move often and create new lines
Every ruler chose a new shape for their kingdom
questions.explanation: The map changed because of shifting kingdoms, British rule, language demands and local tribal/regional needs — real political and social changes.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Statement 1: India's map has remained exactly the same throughout history. Statement 2: States and kingdoms have changed because people's needs and political conditions changed.
options: Both correct; Statement 2 does not explain 1
Statement 1 is incorrect, Statement 2 is correct
Statement 1 is correct, Statement 2 is incorrect
questions.explanation: The map changed many times (1953, 1956, 2000, 2014), so Statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 gives the true reason.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: In which TWO of these years did India's map change, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: 'We know our map changed in 1953, 1956, 2000, and 2014.' 1757 and 1600 relate to the British arriving and ruling.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Select the TWO years of map changes mentioned on the chapter's summary page.
questions.explanation: The map changed in 1953, 1956, 2000 and 2014. 1947 is independence and 1757 the start of British rule.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which TWO are listed as 'core reasons' why India's map changed?
questions.explanation: The summary lists: protect languages and local cultures; support tribal communities and their heritage; ensure fair development by making governance easier.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: According to the summary, how do the map updates affect India today?
options: People must learn one national language only
Princely rulers decide all local development
British governors still make all the laws
People have a local voice through State Governments
questions.explanation: 'People have a local voice through their State Governments… Development reaches more people.'

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: The chapter says different cultures can thrive together while remaining united as one nation.
questions.explanation: This is listed under 'How Does It Affect India Today?' on the summary page.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: The chapter says India's map is now final and can never change again.
questions.explanation: The chapter asks what India's map 'might look like when you grow up? Will there be more states, or fewer?' — it treats the map as 'alive'.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Imagine states were drawn as perfect squares on a chessboard. Which problem might a community face?
options: People of one language could be split across states
Rivers would stop flowing across the state lines
Every state would have exactly equal taxes
The British would come back to rule the squares
questions.explanation: The answer key: 'People of one language could be split into different states' and natural boundaries would be ignored, making governance difficult.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Select the TWO problems the answer key lists if states were drawn as chessboard squares.
options: One language community could be split
Taxes would become impossible to collect
questions.explanation: The key says natural features used as boundaries would be ignored, language groups could be split, and governance would not match people's needs and culture.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: How many States does India have today, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: 'The map was reorganized into 28 States and 8 Union Territories.'

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: The summary says the map was reorganised 'clearing away old lines'. Which old lines?
questions.explanation: The 'old lines' were the British Provinces and Princely State boundaries drawn for tax and trade.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which version of 'India OS' introduced the 'dual-layer system'?
questions.explanation: v2.0 (British rule) was 'Provinces & Princely States — a dual-layer system'.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which 'India OS' version has the system style 'Localised Community Network'?
questions.explanation: v4.0 (2000–Present): '28 States & 8 Union Territories — Localised Community Network'.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which 'India OS' version has the system style 'Shifting Kingdoms & Empires'?
questions.explanation: v1.0, before the British, was 'Shifting Kingdoms & Empires' with no fixed borders.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which TWO statements appear in the book's 'Tick the statement(s) you agree with' box?
options: People's needs can shape state boundaries
Only the British can redraw maps
questions.explanation: The box lists: 'Maps can change over time', 'People's needs can shape state boundaries' and 'Reorganising states can make administration easier'.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: 'Development reaches more people' is listed in the summary as?
options: A reason the British drew provinces
A feature of India OS v1.0
An effect of the map updates today
A problem that crashed the system
questions.explanation: It appears under 'How Does It Affect India Today?' along with people having a local voice.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Sardar Patel merged the Princely States before the States Reorganisation Act of 1956.
questions.explanation: The merger followed independence in 1947; the Act came later in 1956.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which of these events came FIRST?
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh (1953) came first; Jharkhand and Uttarakhand came in 2000 and Telangana in 2014.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which of these events came LAST?
questions.explanation: Telangana (2014) is the latest change; Andhra Pradesh 1953, the Act 1956, Chhattisgarh 2000.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: The chapter's answer to 'Has India always looked like this on a map?' is NO.
questions.explanation: The whole chapter shows the map being 'updated' in v1.0, v2.0, v3.0 and v4.0.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: In the 'My State Home-Screen Designer' activity, Gond art is suggested as an example for which icon?
questions.explanation: Icon 3, the Community/Tribe Widget, asks for 'a symbol of a famous local festival or art style (like Gond art…)'.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which icon in the Home-Screen Designer asks you to draw the state's shape and write its capital?
questions.explanation: Icon 4, the Map Node: 'Draw the geometric shape of the state and write its capital city.'

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which Home-Screen icon would show a famous fort, river or monument?
questions.explanation: Icon 2, the Heritage Vault: 'Draw a famous natural boundary, historical fort, river, or monument found there.'

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: The 'complete your India map' activity asks you to write each state's name, its capital, and what else?
options: One fact you know about the state
The name of its British governor
The king who ruled it long ago
questions.explanation: 'Add one fact you know about the state — something special about its food, festival, monument, language, wildlife, culture, or geography.'

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: Which of these was NOT a reason for a map change in the chapter?
options: Water had to be shared fairly
questions.explanation: Language (1953–56), tribal needs (2000) and water sharing (2014) were real reasons. Natural features do not move and redraw states.

questions.topic: Why India's Map Changed: The Big Picture
questions.question: What does the chapter mean by saying India's map is 'alive'?
options: It is printed on living plants
It moves with the rivers each monsoon
It changes to help people manage resources
It is redrawn every single year
questions.explanation: 'If the map of India is alive and changes to help people look after their resources better…' — the map changes to serve people's needs.
